en: The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, translated by the Western Jin layman Nie Daozhen.
Chapter One: The Five Hindrances. **Chapter One: The Five Hindrances** [Text begins] ... [The remainder of the text follows] ... [End of text]
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha at the Place of Pure Dharma, upon a naturally formed diamond throne. His radiance was exceedingly bright, illuminating everywhere without exception. He sat together with a great assembly of countless bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, among whom the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī were the foremost.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:

"If there are those who seek the path of a bodhisattva—sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to attain unobstructed purity—what dharmas should they practice to bring about that attainment for themselves?"
Samantabhadra replied to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

"If there are good men or good women who wish to seek the bodhisattva path, they should adjust their robes and, three times each day and night, prostrate themselves before the Buddhas of the ten directions. They should pay homage, repent of their transgressions, and regret all the evils they have committed. They should practice patience toward all that ought to be endured, pay homage to all those worthy of homage, aspire to all that is worthy of aspiration, and make requests of all those worthy of being requested. In this way, all such veils of sin, veils of defilement, and veils of phenomena will be entirely removed;
all merits will be fully attained."

“The Prajñāpāramitā, the *Tuṣātapurā-sūtra*, all samādhis, all dhāraṇīs, and all upāyakauśalya—these are the supreme leaders among all sūtras. To [venerate] such as these is to have already paid homage to all Buddhas; this is the ultimate sincerity of one’s intent.”
**Chapter Two: Repentance** The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra said:

"Whatever evil has been committed by my body, whatever transgressions have been made by my speech, and whatever unwholesome thoughts have been conceived by my mind—conceived in all Buddha-fields, as numerous as the atoms therein—all such evils, I now repent for them all:

'Whatever evil I have done since beginningless time toward the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, the Kalyāṇamitras, my parents, the Arhats, the Pratyekabuddhas, the Tathāgatas, the deities of the Tathāgata’s shrines, and within the Dharma of the Tathāgata—all the faults and evils I have committed, I now repent. "

Sukhamatī, if there are any doubts regarding the land of Amitābha Buddha, all Buddhas, all Buddha-lands, or all Buddha-dharmas, and if anyone gives rise to thoughts of disbelief, I shall, on their behalf, repent for all their transgressions.

Should there be anyone who slanders all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, all Karuṇāmaitrīs (Kāruṇikas), all parents, all Arhats, all Pratyekabuddhas, and all people; or who, following their own desires, following their delusions, or following their own self-will, is stubborn and perverse, refusing to speak with others;

or who is dragged by lustful greed, dragged by stinginess and envy, dragged by covetousness, or dragged by flattery—dragged by seven hundred and fifty such desires; when their mind is thus distracted and unable to be self-composed, being covered by all obscurations and terrified by all fears, such that the intentions they give rise to are full of faults.
Now, [I,] so-and-so, repent of all my transgressions.

"From incalculable kalpas ago, I have harbored evil intentions toward the Buddha; or I have caused schisms within the Saṃgha of bhikṣus; or I have harmed arhats; or I have harmed my father or mother; or, upon seeing the True Dharma, I have called it non-Dharma; or, upon seeing what is not the Dharma, I have called it the Dharma; or I have reviled all people; or in my thoughts I have constantly engaged in unrighteous matters;
or regarding the transgressions committed by others, those I intended to commit, or those already committed;..."

If one violates the instructions and admonitions of the Buddha, whatever transgressions and evils have been committed—whether in this life or in previous lives—at a time when one was ignorant of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha of bhikṣus.
Now I, [Name], repent of all my transgressions and faults.

"Whatever thoughts of deviance and envy I have harbored—whether it was to obstruct those who possess the Buddha so that people may not see him, or to obstruct those who clarify the scriptures and preach the Dharma so that people may not hear them; [I now repent of all such deeds]."
If there are kalyāṇamitras who stop people from attending assemblies;
or if they scold and forbid others from giving bowls, robes, food, bedding, or medicine for the sick as meritorious acts, thereby preventing them from doing so;
and if they do not cease such endless interference, but instead continue to incite one another to commit these offenses.
Now, [I], so-and-so, repent of all transgressions and faults.
"Whatever sins I have committed, or when seeing others commit them, I encouraged and assisted them; because of this, I am dragged by my offenses and born in this degenerate age."
If one is born into a poor family;
if one is separated from a kalyāṇamitra;
or if there is a Buddha, yet one is unable to see him.
If there are bodhisattvas who are unable to meet with a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) and are unable to hear the Dharma of the sutras;
because of the various evils they have committed, they are unable to encounter the bodies of these noble sages.
Now, I, [Name], repent for all my transgressions and offenses.
"Whatever sins I have committed, I was unable to hear the Dharma;
or though I heard the Dharma, my mind was unable to receive it."
If, having already received [the teachings], one again forgets them, being unable to firmly uphold the Dharma or clearly maintain the Dharma, and is timid, inferior, and lacking courage;
if their physical form cannot attain an upright and handsome appearance;

if in every birth they always possess little wealth and treasure; if they cannot attain the practice of *dhāraṇī*, cannot attain the practice of *samādhi*, cannot attain the practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*, cannot attain the practice of non-conceptual wisdom (*amanasikāra-jñāna*), cannot attain the wisdom entered through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), and cannot attain the unimpeded wisdom entered through the *Tuṣita-bhira* [or *Tuṣita-vibhūti*].

All the sins one has committed cannot equal this. Now, [I], so-and-so, repent of all transgressions. "Whatever sins I have committed, I am unable to attain the merit of the wisdom that enters into the practice of all dharmas;

I am unable to attain the merit of the wisdom that engages with the intentions of all people; I am unable to attain the merit of the wisdom that enters through the five faculties of all people; I am unable to attain the merit of the wisdom that enters into the discipline of all people; I am unable to attain the merit of the wisdom that enters into all dharmas; I am unable to attain the merit of the wisdom of Nirvana for all people."

All the various sins one has committed cannot compare to this. Now, [I,] so-and-so, repent for all transgressions. "Whatever sins I have committed, I am unable to attain clairvoyance or clairaudience;

I am unable to attain the supernormal power of flying through the air; I am unable to attain knowledge of my own past lives; I am unable to know the affairs of the past and future; I am unable to attain the Brahma-voice; I am unable to attain the merits of body, speech, and mind; I am unable to attain pure and lofty conduct; and I am unable to become fully endowed with merit."
All the various sins one has committed cannot compare to this.
Now, [I], so-and-so, repent of all my transgressions.
"If another person gives rise to an evil intent toward me, or if there is a multitude of soldiers, or if I give rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward that other person;
If there are various armies, or if one encounters all manner of obscurations and fears, may such a person gather before all Buddhas;
with the truth of all eyes and the truth of pervasive wisdom, may their words be immediately accepted as true.

I, [Name], therefore sincerely take refuge before you and repent; I further confess my transgression, having fully acknowledged it and reproached myself, not daring to conceal it. From this day forward, I dare not commit such an offense again.
**Chapter Three: On Aspiration and Delight** The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra said:
“Good sons and good daughters who seek the path of a bodhisattva should form this aspiration and delight: ‘Now I, [Name], take refuge in the All-Knowing One.

To all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, kalyāṇamitras, as well as my parents, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all people, I pray with a sincere heart for compassion. That which cannot be known, may it now be known by me, just as it is known by all the Buddhas.’”
One who takes refuge in this manner has truly taken refuge. Furthermore:

"Now I pay homage to all Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, all Kalyāṇamitras, my parents, and the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; I pay homage to those who are most central, most supreme, unsurpassed, the light among lights, peerless and incomparable, as known by the Buddhas."
One who acts in this manner has already performed the prostration that ought to be made.

Furthermore, I now wish to pay homage to the merit of all Buddhas, the merit of all Bodhisattvas, the merit of all Kāla-mitras, the merit of all Arhats, the merit of all Pratyekabuddhas, and the merit performed by all persons throughout the ten directions, just as it is known by the Buddhas.
In this way, by paying homage to all those meritorious qualities, one has paid homage to them all.
"This is the wisdom of a bodhisattva.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family possesses such merit, they should joyfully aspire to share in their gladness."
If there are those who have attained the Buddha’s wisdom, whatever they should aspire to and delight in, I, so-and-so, already aspire to and delight in that.
As for those who have not yet performed meritorious deeds, may they now perform them; I, so-and-so, aspire to and delight in all of this.
Whatever merit has been performed by those who are honored, and by those even more honored, may I also rejoice in it.
By means of the merit from my own rejoicing, may all beings throughout the ten directions fully attain it.
**Chapter Four: On Exhortation** The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra said:
"Good sons and good daughters who seek the path of a bodhisattva should offer this exhortation:

'I, with a sincere heart, exhort all Buddhas—those Buddhas currently present, those who have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and have reached *avaivartika*, and those who have already fully realized equal knowledge but have not yet turned the wheel of Dharma—I exhort these Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma.'"

Now, as for the turning of the wheel of Dharma by all Buddhas, it is because they employ exhortations and entreaties; thus, the sutras and teachings they proclaim cause all people to each obtain their proper place and bring them all to peace and security.

Furthermore, may all devas, nāgas, ghosts and spirits, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—and those who dwell within the various states of suffering in the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and among the beasts—be brought to liberation.
Those who lack understanding shall all be made to abandon their deluded thoughts and attain right mindfulness, entering the path of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, whenever any Buddhas wish to enter parinirvāṇa, I shall entreat them not to do so for the sake of all people, requesting that they remain for incalculable kalpas, abiding by means of the Dharma-body as one who abides nowhere."
The sūtra teachings he expounds cause all people to each attain their proper place;
they cause them all to be courageous and to fully possess the dharma-practice of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva.
May all people take this as their foundation and each attain peace and security.

Furthermore, may the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the birds and beasts—all who undergo toil and suffering—attain liberation soon.
Those who lack understanding are led to abandon their deluded thoughts and attain right-mindedness, entering the path of the Buddha.
Those who practice what is false are all made to abandon the heterodox paths and enter the true path, so that they all abide in the fundamental state of non-dharmas.
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra said:
"Good sons and good daughters who seek the bodhisattva path should practice giving."
"Whatever merits may be repented of, whatever may be endured, whatever may be venerated, whatever may be aspired to with joy, and whatever merits may be requested or exhorted;

whether they are yet to be performed, are currently being performed, or have already been performed—all such performed merits shall be entirely gathered and accomplished together, becoming a single flavor of merit."
As is the nature of all Buddhas' teachings, and as the Buddhas know it, these merits lead to the attainment of the marks of a Buddha upon rebirth and enable one to achieve the dharma of self-mastery.
Whatever gifts are bestowed, having received such gifts and continuing to bestow them, this giving constitutes right giving, free from attachment and cessation.
I take this merit from the gift of Dharma and cause all people to attain and receive the Dharma, causing them all to resolve their minds upon it.

Just as the giving of Sarvājña (Omniscience) is equal [to all], so now do I give; may it be like the practice of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, and by means of this merit, may I cause all beings to partake in it.
May none of us fall into the hells, among hungry ghosts, or as birds and beasts, nor be born into the eight difficult and evil paths;
may we all be born where there are Buddhas and where there are Bodhisattvas, and may we all be born in the land of Sukhāvatī, the realm of Amitābha Buddha.
"May I, by means of these merits and through my wholesome intention, fully and universally resolve upon the mind of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
'May I, by means of the merit of bestowing this Dharma-gift, act as a shelter and a protector for all people.'"

Having received their refuge, I shall deliver them; I am the light in the darkness, the most brilliant light among all lights; I am the support in that which supports, the most honored support among all supports.
Of all people who have not yet been delivered, I shall deliver them; those who have not yet attained liberation, I shall liberate;
those who have not yet entered parinirvāṇa, I shall cause to enter parinirvāṇa.
"I shall act so as to cause all people to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

'By the merit of my upholding this Dharma and bestowing it upon others, may all people become equal to me in body; in whatever places they are born, and whatever thoughts they may conceive, may they always make offerings to the Buddhas and make offerings to the Bodhisattvas. By means of the aforementioned acts of making offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, may all people, together with my own person, never be separated from the Bodhisattva-dharma, nor be separated from Kāruṇika, Mañjuśrī, Vimalakīrti, Samantabhadra, and the other Bodhisattvas.'"

The practices of these bodhisattvas are all fully endowed with the pure samādhi of dhāraṇī; they are single-minded and unshakable, having accomplished the practice of the prajñāpāramitā, and are entirely proficient in upāyakauśalya (skillful means). Regarding everything they enter among all phenomena, they discern their specific distinctions and cause all people to attain [realization] together with them; such is the perfection of the wisdom-practice of these bodhisattvas.
"By the merit of this Dharma-gift that I hold, may all those who are bound, fettered, and constrained within the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals, be granted liberation."
Those without eyes shall obtain eyes; the deaf shall obtain hearing; and those who are in the midst of toil and suffering shall all attain peace and security.

Whether they be in this Buddha-field or in other Buddha-fields—from the Avīci hell below to the Ultimate Limit (Akanistha) above—among the wriggling creatures therein, whether with feet or without feet, whether born from eggs, from moisture, or by transformation, whether with form or formless, with thought or without thought, and including all humans and non-humans who are mutually dependent and attached: he shall, by means of the Buddha-eye, at the proper time maintain vision, perceive, and fully awaken to them all. He shall cause them all to obtain human form and enter the Buddha-way; having heard the Dharma, they shall all understand and receive it, and all shall attain the mind of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
"May the merit from my holding and bestowing this Dharma-gift cause all people to receive it.

May I, through this merit, fully attain the equal practices of all Buddhas, the practices of all Bodhisattvas, and the practices of all *pāramitās*, so that all people may reach the stage of making offerings and generating vows, attain all Buddha-fields, and be able to purify the dharmas of the three periods of time, understanding them all thoroughly."
It is like a diamond, which penetrates everything without exception.
May I cause all people to receive it, so that they may all attain the wisdom of a Buddha and be fully endowed with all capacities for spiritual transformation, such that they are entirely equal.
May they attain all profound wisdom and be free from doubt regarding all phenomena.

By means of these merits, may [the name of the person] fulfill their vows, and like the Dharma-practice of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, may they fully attain the ten powers and the stages (*bhūmi*).
"Take this as proof.
By means of these merits, I vow that all people and [this person named] so-and-so shall all obtain blessings.
Chapter 5: Parable of Merit (Pǐfú Pǐn) The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī asked the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to seek the Bodhisattva path, and who, three times each day and night, repent of their transgressions and encourage others to delight in the practice of the Dharma as described above—what would their merit be?"
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra replied to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī:

“If there are sons or daughters of good family who practice the bodhisattva path, and they were to fill the entire land of Jambudvīpa with the seven treasures to offer as alms to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, it would not equal the merit of these sons or daughters of good family who, three times each day and night, encourage others to delight in the practice of the Dharma: repenting what should be repented of, enduring what should be endured, paying homage to what should be honored, aspiring to what should be aspired to, exhorting and inviting others to do the same, and practicing giving as is appropriate—thus following the aforementioned instructions day and night.”

The merit derived from this offering exceeds that of filling Jambudvīpa with the seven treasures and making offerings to a Tathāgata by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, a hundred-millionfold, or even a hundred-billionfold; it can never be compared, calculated, or illustrated.
When this Dharma was being taught, innumerable devas dwelling in the void of space offered celestial flowers, incense, and music as an offering, scattering them over the Buddha and the bodhisattvas.

When the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra had finished preaching this sutra, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, humans, and non-humans, having heard the sutra, were greatly delighted; they came forward, prostrated themselves before the Buddha, and departed.
The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.
